title: Elements • Book III • Proposition 37
subtitle: Converse of the Tangent-Secant Theorem
Visual description: Given circle ABC, external point D, secant DCA, and segment DB falling on the circle at B such that rect(AD, CD) = sq(DB).
narration: Elements, Book three, Proposition thirty-seven. From a point outside a circle, if a secant cuts the circle and another line falls on the circle such that the rectangle contained by the whole secant and its external segment equals the square on the line falling on the circle, then that line touches the circle. From external point D, let secant D C A cut circle A B C, and let segment D B fall on the circumference at B so that the rectangle A D by C D equals the square on D B. We claim that D B is tangent to circle A B C.

subslides.enunciation: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two straight lines, if one of them cut the circle, and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference be equal to the square on the straight line which falls on the circle, the straight line which falls on it will touch the circle.

title: Auxiliary Tangent & Radii
subtitle: Construction
Visual description: Draw tangent DE touching circle ABC at E, find center F, and join FE, FB, and FD; by III.18, angle FED is a right angle.
narration: Using Book three Proposition seventeen, draw a tangent D E from D touching circle A B C at E. Find the center F of the circle, and join segments F E, F B, and F D. Because D E is tangent to the circle at E, Book three Proposition eighteen shows that radius F E is perpendicular to D E, making angle F E D a right angle.

title: Congruence & Right Angle at the Circumference
subtitle: Demonstration
Visual description: By III.36, rect(AD, CD) = sq(DE) = sq(DB), so DE = DB; by SSS (I.8), <FBD ≃ <FED so <DBF = right, and by III.16 Porism DB touches the circle.
narration: By the tangent-secant theorem in Book three Proposition thirty-six, the rectangle A D by C D equals the square on tangent D E. Since the rectangle A D by C D also equals the square on D B by hypothesis, the square on D E equals the square on D B, and therefore segment D E equals segment D B. In triangles F E D and F B D, radii F E and F B are equal, segments D E and D B are equal, and base F D is common. By Side-Side-Side congruence, angle D B F equals the right angle F E D. Since D B stands at right angles to radius F B at its extremity B on the circle, the Porism to Book three Proposition sixteen proves that D B touches circle A B C, as was required to prove.

title: Constructive Converse & Dependency Graph
subtitle: Commentary & Genealogy
Visual description: Commentary on Euclid's constructive converse method (avoiding reductio ad absurdum) and the G.145 genealogy card.
narration: Proposition thirty-seven is the final proposition of Book three, sealing the theory of circles with an algebraic criterion for tangency: instead of proving by contradiction that D B cannot cut the circle a second time, Euclid constructs an auxiliary tangent D E and transfers its right angle to B by triangle congruence. In the GEOMETOR dependency graph, Proposition thirty-seven crowns Book three with sixty-three ancestor nodes, and joins Proposition thirty-six to drive Book four Proposition ten—where this exact tangency criterion proves that a chord equal to the golden section of a radius is tangent to the circumcircle of the smaller triangle, unlocking the regular pentagon.

subslides.commentary_title: Direct Converse via Auxiliary Tangent (Like I.48)
subslides.commentary_body: Just as Euclid proves the converse of the Pythagorean theorem (I.48) by constructing an auxiliary right angle rather than using proof by contradiction, here he constructs an auxiliary tangent / D E / (III.17), deduces / D E / = / D B / via III.36, and transfers the right angle at E to B by I.8 regardless of whether / D C A / passes through the center.
